The Rich Man and Lazarus
LAZ-a-rus
noun phrase
From the Greek of Christ’s account in Luke, naming the beggar Lazarus (Hebrew Eleazar, “God hath helped”) over against the unnamed rich man.

Biblical Definition

Our Lord told of a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day; and a beggar named Lazarus, full of sores, laid at his gate (Luk 16:19; Luk 16:20). The beggar died, and was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom; the rich man also died, and was buried. And in hell he lift up his eyes, being in torments, and seeth Abraham afar off, and Lazarus in his bosom (Luk 16:23). He cried for Lazarus to cool his tongue, for he was tormented in this flame; but Abraham answered that between us and you there is a great gulf fixed, so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot (Luk 16:26). The rich man then begged that Lazarus warn his five brethren, but was told, They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them (Luk 16:29). The dictionary marks this account as our Lord’s own plain teaching upon the state of the dead. He sets before us conscious bliss for the believing poor and conscious torment for the unbelieving rich, a gulf fixed and impassable, and the sufficiency of the written Word. So the Scripture teaches that the soul lives on past death in joy or in woe, that there is no passing over from the one estate to the other, and that they who will not hear Moses and the prophets, neither will be persuaded though one rose from the dead.

Webster 1828 Definition

Our Lord’s account of the rich man in torment and the beggar in Abraham’s bosom, with the great gulf fixed between.

expand to see more

THE RICH MAN AND LAZARUS, our Lord’s account of two men in the state after death.

The rich man fared sumptuously, while Lazarus the beggar lay at his gate.

Lazarus was carried into Abraham’s bosom; the rich man lift up his eyes in torments.

A great gulf is fixed, so that none may pass from the one estate to the other.

Abraham bids the lost trust Moses and the prophets, the written Word.

Key Scripture

Luk 16:22 — "And it came to pass, that the beggar died, and was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom: the rich man also died, and was buried;"

Luk 16:23 — "And in hell he lift up his eyes, being in torments, and seeth Abraham afar off, and Lazarus in his bosom."

Luk 16:26 — "And beside all this, between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot; neither can they pass to us, that would come from thence."

Luk 16:31 — "And he said unto him, If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead."

Modern Corruption

The denial of eternal conscious punishment, treating Christ’s account as “just a parable” to evade His plain teaching.

expand to see more

A real corruption of this passage is the denial of eternal conscious punishment, whether by the annihilationist who would have the lost extinguished, or by the universalist who teaches that God will eventually save all and empty hell at the last. To escape the plain force of our Lord’s words, the corruption styles this account “just a parable,” as though a parable might not teach truth, and so dismisses the torment, the flame, and the great gulf fixed as mere imagery carrying no doctrine of the world to come.

The dictionary rebuts this on the text and on the authority of Christ Himself. Whether this be a true history or a parable, it is the Lord’s own teaching, and He does not teach by falsehood; the conscious torment, the lifting up of the eyes, the cry for one drop of water, the memory and the longing, are set before us by Him who knoweth the state of the dead. He says plainly that the gulf is fixed, so that none may pass over; there is no second chance, no purgatorial cleansing, no final restoration. The plea that God’s love would not allow such a thing is not Scripture but sentiment set against Scripture; the same Christ who is the Saviour is the Judge, and His word here stands. The lost are warned, while the day of grace lasts, to hear Moses and the prophets, for after death the gulf cannot be crossed.

Hebrew Roots

From the Greek account of Lazarus and the rich man, teaching conscious bliss and conscious torment after death.

expand to see more

The Rich Man and Lazarus — Lazarus, from Hebrew Eleazar, “God hath helped.”

Our Lord sets two men before us in the state after death.

Lazarus rests in Abraham’s bosom; the rich man is in torments.

A great gulf is fixed, impassable from either side.

They who hear not Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded though one rose.

Usage

"As in the account of the rich man and Lazarus, the soul lives on past death in joy or in woe."

"Between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass cannot."

"If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded though one rose from the dead."
